fullPassage: The early Earth collided with numerous other masses during its formation; indeed, the proto-Earth is thought to have sustained a massive impact with a Mars-sized body named 'Theia'. The Moon probably formed from this collision about 100 million years after the formation of the solar system. This impact is thought to have knocked the Earth off its 'daily' rotational axis so that the Earth now tilts about 23.4° away from its orbital axis around the Sun, although there is a slight 'wobble' of a few degrees. This 23.4° tilt, as we orbit around the Sun, causes our yearly cycle of the seasons. During part of the year, the northern hemisphere is tilted towards the Sun (summer) and the southern hemisphere is tilted away (winter). Six months later, the situation is reversed. Critically, the Moon's gravitational pull stabilizes the Earth's axial tilt, moderating the degree of wobble. This has produced a relatively stable climate on Earth for billions of years, and many believe that life on Earth would never have got started without this stabilization by the Moon. To rephrase a song from the 1970s, we are all children of the Moon.
